title: Positioning on training and professionalism
audience: Owners and team leaders who want more repeat and referred work by showing how their team is trained and how it behaves on site.
learningOutcomes: Define a market position in one sentence tied to a customer need
Convert a training program into a visible, evidenced promise
Write a damage response the team can use on site

instruction.heading: What positioning means
instruction.body: Positioning is the reason a particular customer picks your business over a similar service. It is not a slogan. Both sample documents position the business on trained staff and professional conduct. The business plan puts training first. The proposal extends the standard from the first greeting through to the way damage is handled. Positioning built on training works only when customers can see the training, and only when the team behaves the same way on every job.

instruction.heading: Make training visible
instruction.body: The sample plan describes three kinds of training: a method for doing the work, working effectively in a team, and a continuing learning system. Each can become a promise. 'Every new team member completes a documented induction before working unsupervised' is a promise you can keep and show. 'Our staff are highly trained professionals' is not. Keep the induction record, the method sheets and the refresher dates, and be ready to show them when a client asks what training their team has had.

instruction.heading: Professionalism happens at specific moments
instruction.body: The sample proposal treats professional conduct as something that runs through the whole visit: the greeting, the handling of access, the way the work is done, and what happens when something is damaged. Write down those moments for your own team. For each one, state the expected behaviour in a sentence or two. The damage moment matters most, because it is when customer doubt is highest. Write a short response process before the first job: stop, make safe, tell the client the same day, record the damaged item with photos, and follow the agreed resolution steps. Brief every team member on it and rehearse it.

instruction.heading: Appearance and the look of professionalism
instruction.body: The sample plans use uniforms and magnetic signs on vehicles to create an impression of professionalism. Any uniform or vehicle signage only works if it matches the team that arrives. A branded vehicle with an untidy crew sends a mixed message. Check that the signage shows the business name the client will recognise, that uniforms are clean and fitted, and that vehicles are roadworthy and parked with care. Rules on vehicle signage and advertising are set by each state or territory, so check the local rule in each one where you work.

instruction.heading: Environmental products as a supporting message
instruction.body: For example, a cleaning sample plan written for another country, at an undated time, says its chemicals are environmentally sound. That is not an Australian fact. The plan also notes that other companies use similar products, so the claim is not a major point of difference. Use it as a supporting message only, and only after checking it. Any environmental or green claim must match the product's documentation. The ACCC's guidance on false or misleading claims covers 'green' and 'non-toxic' claims and expects them to be based on reasonable grounds. Check the safety data sheet and the supplier's technical information, and write down which products the claim covers. Do not describe a product as green or safe in general terms if the documents only cover some of its uses.

instruction.heading: Protect the message
instruction.body: Every promise in marketing is a commitment the team must keep on every job. Review the promises each quarter against the records: training records, complaints, damage reports and client feedback. If a promise is not being kept, either change the promise or fix the practice before you advertise it again.

procedure: List the three to five promises you want to make about training and professionalism.
For each promise, write the site behaviour that delivers it.
For each behaviour, name the record that proves it.
Write the arrival, greeting and damage responses as short numbered steps.
Brief every team member and record the date of the briefing.
Review the promises against the records every quarter.

workedExamples.situation: A team of three wants to charge a premium for 'fully trained professionals'. Two of the three started within the last month and have completed only the first part of the induction. The owner is the only person who has run a full site job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the business claim 'fully trained professionals' now, and what promise can it make instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: The claim is not supported, because not every team member has completed induction and not every member has supervised experience. A supported promise is 'every team member completes a documented induction and works with a supervisor until signed off'. The owner names the supervising person and dates the sign-off. The stronger claim can follow once the records support it.

equipmentAndPpe: Product safety data sheet folder, for any chemicals or products used

commonErrors.error: Making a training claim the records do not support
commonErrors.prevention: Attach the training record to the claim, and change the claim if the record does not match.

commonErrors.error: Calling a product green or safe in general terms
commonErrors.prevention: Check the safety data sheet and technical data for each product, and keep the claim to what it covers.

commonErrors.error: Having no damage process until damage happens
commonErrors.prevention: Write and brief the process before the first job, and rehearse it.

commonErrors.error: Promising professionalism with no site standard behind it
commonErrors.prevention: Turn each promise into a behaviour the team can be checked against.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Advertising claims about products, safety and environmental benefit must not mislead. The ACCC's guidance on false or misleading claims says claims should be true, accurate and based on reasonable grounds, and that a business must be able to prove them.

Use products as their label and safety data sheet state, with the PPE they list. Mixing products, or using them outside their stated uses, is a hazard. Chemical safety duties come from work health and safety laws, which are set by each state or territory, so check the rules that apply where you work.
Rules on vehicle signage and vehicle advertising vary by state or territory, so check the local rule in each state or territory where you work before relying on this point.

qualityStandard: Every public claim about training, conduct or products has a matching record or document.
Each team member has a dated induction record and a named supervisor until sign-off.
The damage response is written, briefed to all staff, and rehearsed.
Promises are reviewed quarterly against the records.
documentationEvidence: Induction and training records for each team member
Damage report, with photos and client sign-off
Safety data sheet register and claims register
summary: Positioning on training works only when customers can see the training record.
Professionalism is a set of specific moments, and the damage moment is critical.
Environmental claims must match the product documentation.
Review every promise against the records, and change any promise the records do not support.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which training claim is best supported for use in marketing?
options: A documented induction record for each team member that matches the claim, with a named supervisor
Our team members are fully trained and every one of them has been assessed for the job
Our training is better than our competitors' training and our staff have more hours of training each year
Our uniforms show that we are trained and that the uniform is always clean and pressed

knowledgeChecks.question: A team uses plant-based products and wants to call them the greenest on the market. What should happen first?
options: Publish the claim now on the website and in every advert, straight away, for all clients
Stop using the products altogether and tell every client about the change this week
Check the product safety data sheet and technical information, and keep the claim to what it supports
Let the client decide the wording of the greenest claim on the market for their own site

knowledgeChecks.question: Why write a damage response before the first job?
options: So staff can avoid reporting damage and nobody needs to know about it
So the team responds the same way under pressure, and the client knows the process
So prices can rise after damage and the client pays for every item
So insurance is not needed and the team can work without any plan at all
